title: Guntur Taluk — historical narrative notes from Census 1961
method: Concise source-grounded notes extracted from the locality sections. Legends and oral traditions remain explicitly attributed to the source.

notes: The source records Amareswara and numerous subsidiary deities within the temple compounds.
It describes inscriptions associated with Amareswara, including Saka 1104 and Saka 1283 references, and later patronage by Sri Krishna Devaraya and Raja Vasireddy Venkatadri Naidu.
Mahasivaratri/Sri Amareswaraswamy festival is recorded as a ten-day observance.
Sri Venkateswaraswamy, Perumallaswamy and Ramaswamy are recorded as places of worship.
The Venkateswara observance is described from Magham to Vaisakham on Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays, with several offerings and ceremonial uses of the temple.
The source says the village was formerly called Buddha-viramam and preserves a traditional explanation for a later name change.
It records a tradition connecting Raja Vasireddy Venkatadri Naidu with construction of the Venkateswara temple and the settlement of sixty Vaishnava Brahmin families.
A Bhairavaswamy image at Bhairava Dibba and reported Buddhist-age marble images are also noted.
The source connects the name Velagapudi with wood-apple gardens and the word Velaga.
Sri Rama Mandir, Someswaraswamy, Anjaneyaswamy and Veera Malleswaraswamy are recorded, along with village-deity shrines.
Rama Kalyanam, Someswara worship, Anjaneya offerings and Veera Malleswara abhishekam are described.
The source records Sri Lakshmi Narasimhaswamy Theppothsavam, a one-day boat festival in Magham.
The source connects Gundemeda with the historical Kandravadi country and references Eastern Chalukya inscriptions and Kota chiefs.
Kasi Visweswara, Venugopala, Ganganamma, Anjaneya and Rama worship are recorded.
Sri Sivakesavula Uthsavam is described as an ancient local festival.
Sri Venugopalaswamy temple and a two-day Magham Uthsavam are recorded; the source states that about 1,000 Hindu devotees participated.
Venugopalaswamy temple, Brahmamgari mutt and a Siva temple are recorded.
Venugopalaswamy Kalyanothsavam is described as a five-day festival with Kalyanam and Rathothsavam.
The source records a former fort and explains a traditional Vippatam-to-Ippatam name change using the word vippukunta.
Bhramaramba Malleswaraswamy temple and Rama Mandir are recorded; Mollempudi has Venugopalaswamy and Rama worship.
The Bhramaramba Malleswara festival is described as ancient and locally significant.
The source translates Mangalagiri as 'the auspicious hill'.
It records 1520 and 1558 inscriptional evidence near the temple and discusses competing accounts of the large gopuram's construction.
Panakala Lakshmi Narasimhaswamy, Venkateswara, Lakshmi, Rajyalakshmi, Rama, Malleswara and Lakshminarayana worship are described.
The source records the Panakala offering tradition, Brahmothsavam and other major festivals. Legends are retained as legends rather than verified history.
The source gives the former name Vathsavayipalem and associates it with Vathsavayi rulers before describing the later settlement as Pedaparimi.
Malleswara-Bhramaramba, Rama, Anjaneya, Vinayaka, Poleramma and Venugopala worship are recorded.
Malleswara-Bhramaramba Kalyanothsavam and Venugopala Rukmini Kalyanam are described as ancient local festivals.
The source records a three-foot stone Veeranjaneyaswamy image in Kamaiah Thopu.

It says the image originally belonged to a temple in neighboring Thurlapadu; after that village was deserted and the temple fell into ruin, the image was exposed and was moved to Ravela in 1937 by the Seetharamanjaneya Society under Subba Rao.
Sri Rama, Poleramma, Maha Lakshmamma, Venugopalaswamy and Anjaneya worship are also recorded.
The source records Srirama Navami as a two-day local observance in Chaitra Suddha Navami and Dasami.
The source attributes the festival statement to the Superintendent of Police, Guntur.
The source records a three-day Guru Sydula Urs during Ramzan and says local devotees congregated without distinction of caste or creed.
The Census map index separately lists Sri Venkateswara Swamy for Perecherla's Ashada festival entry.
The source says Nidumukkala was under the rule of Vijayanagara kings and the Reddys of Kondavidu.
The Census map index lists Venkateswara Swamy and an Ashada festival for Nidumukkala.
